title: Vaccine sign-up surge
brief: A county opens 80,000 vaccine appointments at 8 am. Within seconds, thousands of people reload and bots try to grab slots. The site must stay up, never sell the same slot twice, and be fair to people on a phone with a poor signal.

clarify.q: How many people show up at once?
clarify.a: About forty times the usual traffic for the first fifteen minutes after 8 am, then it falls back.

clarify.q: Is it fine to make people wait?
clarify.a: Yes, if it is fair and clear. A short wait is better than an error page. Failing and reloading makes it worse.
Yes. Scripts try to book many slots and resell them. About half as much bot traffic as human traffic shows up a few minutes in.

clarify.q: What if the database fails mid-rush?
clarify.a: Bookings must not be lost or doubled. A short stall is acceptable; a wrong slot count is not.

requirements.users: 4 million residents; 600,000 try on launch day (approx.)
notes: Base traffic is about a tenth of the peak number; the 8 am rush multiplies it.
The event is a one-off, so capacity you rent for an hour counts only for an hour.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Slot booking attempts in the rush

hints: The slot list is the same for everyone. Which element can answer thousands of people with one copy that is a few seconds old?
A rate limiter protects the rest from bots and from people reloading. It turns hard failure into a polite "try again".
Durable booking identity makes retries safe and lets clients recover confirmation. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The rush is 40 times normal and lasts a quarter hour. The answer is to refuse some load gently, copy the answers that are the same for everyone, and protect the one thing that has to be exact: the slot count.

designs.name: Limit, copy, scale, keep one truth
designs.why: A CDN holds the slot list for a few seconds. A WAF and rate limiter drop bots and reloaders. The app autoscales behind a load balancer; the SQL primary (XL, synchronous, two zones) owns the slot count; a replica serves lists. Notices and analytics go through a queue.

tradeoffs: A 5-second CDN copy of the slot list may show a slot that has just gone. The booking step is the source of truth, so the worst case is a polite "that slot was just taken".
The rate limiter will turn away a few honest people who reload quickly. That is the price of keeping the site up for everyone else.
A bigger single database (XL) is simple and holds everything in one place, but it is one box; the failover takes about a minute and bookings pause meanwhile.
A waiting room (a queue in front of the whole site) is the fairest design, and costs the most to build; this design is the lean alternative.
editorial.realWorld: Public vaccine sites in 2021 regularly saw 20 to 100 times their usual traffic within a minute of slots opening (approx.), and the ones that stayed up usually put a queue or waiting room in front and cached everything that was the same for all visitors.

correctness.prompt: Two people book the last available slot at once. What schema constraint and transaction would allow only one booking?
correctness.discussion: Identify the scarce resource and time range. Enforce uniqueness for fixed slots, or prevent overlapping reservations with a database constraint or serializable transaction. Check availability and create the reservation atomically in the authoritative store. Cached availability is only a hint. Give each booking request a stable key so retries return the original booking rather than consume another slot. A stable signed admission token protects fairness for weak connections. Admission limits pressure; it does not enforce booking uniqueness. Durable booking identity makes retries safe and lets clients recover confirmation.

fields.label: Step 1. A phone reconnects after getting waiting token W. What place does it get?
options: Resume W subject to expiry and abuse controls
Send the phone to the end on every retry
fields.explanation: A stable signed admission token protects fairness for weak connections.

fields.label: Step 2. Two admitted users claim the final slot. What decides?
options: An atomic slot claim and unique booking key in the authoritative store
fields.explanation: Admission limits pressure; it does not enforce booking uniqueness.

fields.label: Step 3. The winning booking loses its reply. What should retry do?
options: Reserve a second slot because the first result is missing
Return the existing booking under the original key
fields.explanation: Durable booking identity makes retries safe and lets clients recover confirmation.

correctness.responsibility: Allocate each appointment once while preserving fair retryable admission.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
